extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of European intellectual and religious history
extracted.subtask_description: Historical-analysis of the social, intellectual, institutional, and political causes that produced the conversion of the Roman Empire to Christianity and the nature/causes of related persecutions. The page surveys factors of appeal, organisational strength, ritual incentives, and state responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidential system had no prominent place
rubrics_metrics.description: “What is called the evidential system had no prominent place in effecting the conversion of the Roman Empire.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical criticisms were too imperfect to make appeals to past miracles valuable; alleged miracles were often private and unimpressive; therefore appeals to evidential miracles were of subsidiary importance in conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: General tendencies of the age as primary causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The main causes of conversion are to be sought in the 'vast movement of mingled scepticism and credulity,' the 'amalgamation or dissolution of many creeds,' and the 'profound transformation of habits, of feelings, and of ideals' of the age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under widespread social/intellectual fluidity and religious pluralism, religions competed for adherents in Rome where many faiths and philosophies coexisted; Christianity's fit with contemporary spiritual needs made its success largely inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christianity combined many distinct elements of power and attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity uniquely combined elements that made it attractive across classes: not bound by local ties, appealed to the affections, offered sympathetic worship, had a pure and noble ethical system, proclaimed universal brotherhood, and connected with both slaves and philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Judaism (local/national), Stoicism (cold, impractical), and Egyptian mystery cults (lacked ethical system). Christianity's teachings matched the moral sentiments of the time and addressed emotional and social needs ('more concerned with modes of feeling than with modes of thought').

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious prodigy and wonder-working enhanced appeal (subsidiary)
rubrics_metrics.description: To a world thirsting for prodigy, Christianity 'offered a history replete with wonders' and had exorcists and legends of continual miracles, which made it attractive to many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though impressive to some classes, these wonders are treated as subsidiary to broader social and moral attractions. The Sibyl prophecies and exorcisms had some weight because of their links to revered authority and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional organisation, exclusivity, and corporate discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Christianity was 'definitely, elaborately, and skilfully organised' and emphatically exclusive; adherents were bound to abjure surrounding faiths, producing 'a stern, aggressive, and at the same time disciplined enthusiasm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public worship duties, sacraments as 'oaths of the Christian warrior,' fasts, penances, commemorative days and the intervention of religion in life events all strengthened Church feeling and sustained collective devotion—advantages isolated teachers lacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of salvation by belief as a central motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that salvation depended on belief and that those outside were 'doomed to an eternity of torture' supplied a motive of action 'as powerful as it is perhaps possible to conceive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teaching struck both hope and fear chords, encouraging conversion by prudential calculation and inspiring fervent evangelism and sacrifice among believers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martyrdom, confession, and relic-cult as social incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessors and martyrs enjoyed high authority and glory; martyrs were buried with splendour, relics were venerated, anniversaries celebrated, and the 'baptism of blood' erased sins—creating strong incentives for martyrdom and public devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: St. Perpetua's martyrdom; public commemoration of martyrs' sufferings; the social and spiritual rewards attached to martyrdom encouraged heroic enthusiasm and willingness to suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive zeal and epidemic desire for martyrdom (social dynamic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain conditions martyrdom 'became at times a form of absolute madness, a kind of epidemic of suicide,' prompting Church leaders to restrain followers from seeking execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary observers (Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius, Lucian) noted Christian indifference to death; authorities sometimes executed some willing martyrs and dismissed others to quell the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persecution often stems from belief in exclusive salvation and the guilt of error
rubrics_metrics.description: A major cause of Christian persecution was the theological doctrine that 'correct theological opinions are essential to salvation' and that theological error 'necessarily involves guilt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two beliefs explain much Christian persecution: they made punitive measures seem both legitimate and necessary, were defended in theological literature, and only declined as theological latitudinarianism and distinctions between fundamentals/non-fundamentals grew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary theological influences promoting persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of theological ethics derived from writings that enjoined religious massacres or elevated the duty of suppressing idolatry, and the representation of the destiny awaiting the misbeliever was 'so ghastly' that earthly suffering in extirpating error was de-emphasised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources furnished moral and rhetorical ammunition that made persecution more readily justifiable in many periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives for persecution are multiple and must be examined case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Persecution may be undertaken for moral, religious, political, or corrupt reasons; from the fact of persecution alone one cannot infer the persecutor's principles without detailed examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical analysis should identify which combination of motives (immorality suppression, offense to deity, state security, personal gain) drove each persecution episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between liberty of speculation and control of ritual
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Roman world speculative freedom (philosophy, criticism) was often wide, while ritual or official religious observances were placed under government control and made matters of compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: philosophers enjoyed freedom of inquiry; the State regulated ritual practices as civic duties tied to prosperity; refusal to perform public rites could be seen as political disloyalty (e.g., incense to emperor statues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman policy evolved from suppression to practical tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Although early Republican laws and occasional suppressions targeted foreign cults, by the Empire (from Tiberius onward) Rome largely granted 'perfect liberty of worship' to most religions, with the ritual obligations of the state remaining an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities sometimes tacitly permitted, sometimes expressly authorised new creeds; enforcement varied with perceived threats to public order, morality, or state unity (examples: Isis/Serapis suppression and later toleration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual conformity seen as civic loyalty; Jews/Christians' refusal provoked tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation to perform the sacred rites of the state religion was regarded as connected with public prosperity; refusal (as by Jews and Christians) could be treated as a refusal of civic duties, arousing hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Jews were often tolerated and even accommodated (e.g., Augustus changed grain distribution day to respect Sabbath), Christians' refusal to burn incense before emperor statues produced similar societal suspicion and sometimes persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance expands with the distinction between fundamental and non-fundamental doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Toleration began when thinkers drew a clear line between fundamental and non-fundamental doctrines; as latitudinarianism spread, toleration increased and persecution waned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rise of parties opposed to ecclesiastical orthodoxy and the growth of indifference to dogma among legislators correlated with the retreat of persecution; revision of theological arguments followed changes in political and intellectual climate.
